1:
Whether these verses begin a book or continue one is answered in opposite ways from the same evidence. Ellicott holds the divisions of the Pentateuch to be anything but arbitrary: Genesis ends naturally where the history of the individuals who founded the nation stops, and the history of the nation itself properly begins at the seventh verse, the six before it forming a connecting link which would not have been needed at all unless this book had been issued as a distinct work, since they are little more than a recapitulation of what Genesis had already said more fully. Gill draws the contrary inference from the first word: the book is joined to the former by the copulative and, and it is highly probable that when this was written no division of the books had been made and the history ran on in one continued account. Keil and Clarke both note the two names the book carries, the Hebrew one taken from its opening words and the Greek from the first half of its contents, Clarke adding that one great codex calls it the departure from Egypt.

The two who date the book's span contradict each other outright. Keil says it embraces three hundred and sixty years, from the death of Joseph at the close of Genesis to the building of the tabernacle at the beginning of the second year after the departure. Clarke, marking the identical termini, says the history covers a hundred and forty-five years. Neither notices the other's figure, and nothing in either account explains the difference.

The seventy souls are handled three ways. Ellicott alone does the arithmetic, making the number up as Jacob himself, his twelve sons, his daughter, fifty-one grandsons, one granddaughter and four great-grandsons; he observes that the other daughters and granddaughters are excluded, that if the female descendants were as numerous as the male the whole issue of his loins would have been a hundred and thirty-two, and that adding the wives of sons and grandsons, the husbands of the daughters and a liberal allowance for retainers carries the party that entered Egypt far higher. Calvin says only that the reckoning is perfectly accurate, and refers to the two other places where the total is given. Gill states the purpose of the notice, that a small number went down compared with the number that came out, and that the comparison is what it is there for. Henry finds a further significance, that seventy was exactly the number of the nations by which the earth was peopled, on the principle that when the Most High separated the sons of Adam he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. Wesley gives the same observation in the same order and very nearly the same words, so the two are not two witnesses here but one.

How large the households were divides two more. Ellicott takes the word in its eastern sense, including not only children and grandchildren but retainers and servants born in the house, like those of Abraham, so that each household may have been very considerable; Wesley confines it to children and grandchildren. Wesley also explains the order of the names, Benjamin standing before Dan and Naphtali because those were the sons of the handmaids. Calvin supplies the frame the whole passage stands in: the descent into Egypt might have looked at the time like the end and abolition of the covenant, and the increase is the proof that God accomplished in his own time what he had promised about the seed. Keil makes the same point from the vocabulary, the words for their fruitfulness pointing back to the blessing given at the creation and after the flood, so that both blessings are here fully realised, and the land they filled is Goshen.
8:
Who the new king was produces four candidates and one refusal. Gill assembles the older opinions — that he was of another family, not of the royal seed, the first of the shepherd kings, or Ramesses Miamun of the ancient house — and sets out a succession of Egyptian reigns from Joseph's arrival. Clarke names Ramesses Miamun or his son and dates him. Ellicott reviews the moderns, some proposing the founder of the eighteenth dynasty and others the greatest king of the nineteenth, and declares for Seti, not that dynasty's founder but the originator of its greatness. Keil declines the question on a point of language: a new king means one who follows different principles of government, as new gods elsewhere means other than the fathers worshipped, so a change of dynasty cannot be inferred from the word, however probable on other grounds.

What it is not to know Joseph divides them further. Clarke makes the verb mean acknowledge or approve, as it often does and as its Greek equivalents do, so the king is not ignorant of Joseph but repudiates him, disapproving the system he had established and refusing to own what Egypt owed him. Henry keeps to forgetting, and turns it into a warning: all who knew him loved him and were kind to his relations for his sake, but when he was dead he was soon forgotten. Wesley gives that sentence almost word for word, so the two are one witness here and not two, though he adds an application of his own, that work done for men dies with us while work done for God follows us. Calvin proposes a cause nobody else does, that the ingratitude grew out of Joseph's own moderation, since had he demanded privileges and immunity from tribute the debt would have been remembered. Ellicott infers from the same clause that the memory of Joseph's benefits had for a considerable time after his death protected his kinsfolk.

Whom the king addressed is disputed in a smaller way. Clarke supposes a council of nobles summoned to consider the matter, and Calvin a public assembly of the kind kings hold, the proposal being laid before the estates. Ellicott denies any assembly is meant: his people stands opposed to the people of the children of Israel and marks only that those addressed were of his own nation, no doubt his courtiers. He then tests the king's statement and finds it false, since Egypt must have held seven or eight millions, implying near two millions of adult men, where the adult Israelites a century later numbered six hundred thousand. Keil and Calvin both note that the verb for dealing wisely is used here of craft, Calvin observing that the word is far more often used in a good sense than a bad one.

On the taskmasters the readings differ by rank and by aim. Ellicott distinguishes two grades in the Egyptian forced-labour system, the overseers who drove the labourers and the superintendents who assigned the work, and identifies these officers with the higher grade. Gill and Clarke make them masters of tribute, Clarke suspecting the people were both worked unmercifully and taxed exorbitantly, and reporting a conjecture that the first of the three names is a city rather than a description. Calvin argues the injustice from the terms of settlement: they ought to have considered on what conditions the Israelites had been admitted, so the exaction broke faith, and the greater crime was that the object was not revenue but affliction. Wesley lists the aims at length — to break their spirits, ruin their health, shorten their days, discourage marriage since the children would be born to slavery, and drive them to abandon their own people — and fears the oppression carried many of them into Egyptian worship.
12:
That the affliction produced the opposite of what it intended is agreed, and the accounts of why differ. Ellicott says flatly that the result was not natural and can only be ascribed to a superintending providence, since severe and constant labour ordinarily exhausts a nation and thins it. Clarke reads the Hebrew as strictly proportional — as they afflicted them, so they multiplied and so they grew — and pushes the proportion further than the text does, that had the sufferings been greater the increase would have been more abundant still. Gill describes the mechanism the Egyptians expected and the one they got: hard labour was meant to break their strength and unfit them for begetting children, and instead it made them healthier and stronger; and he turns this into a rule about afflictive dispensations generally, comparing the palm tree, which grows the more for the weight laid on it. Calvin reads the same verse as a contest between the mercy of God and the cruelty of the king, in which the design against the Church was frustrated, and draws from it both a hope, that what the wicked imagine will come to nothing because God's hand is greater, and a duty, to bear afflictions patiently and rise under the weight. Wesley generalises furthest, that times of affliction have often been the Church's growing times and that Christianity spread most when it was persecuted. Ellicott adds that the word for the Egyptians' vexation is not strong enough in English and should be rendered that they were sore distressed.

On the rigour of the service Clarke makes the sharpest point. The word means ferocity and great oppression, and the same word appears in the later law which forbids an Israelite to rule over his brother with rigour — so the very term describing Egypt's treatment of Israel is the one Israel is afterwards forbidden to deserve. Gill takes the word of what breaks a man's strength, and adds ill words and probably blows to the burdens. Ellicott supplies the documentary picture: forced labour in Egypt meant working from morning to night under a rod freely applied to the legs and back if a man rested a moment, in great heat and with heavy burdens, and death often followed, one king being said by a Greek historian to have destroyed a hundred and twenty thousand of his own subjects in this way. Calvin observes what the failure did to the oppressors, that far from being moved to kindness by their fears they were hardened and spurred to greater cruelty, the wicked not perceiving that God is against them when their strivings come to nothing.

At the last verse two of them describe the work itself. Clarke divides the brickmaking into its stages, the digging and kneading of the clay, the forming and drying of the bricks, then the carrying of materials and the serving of the builders. Ellicott meets an objection instead: it has been questioned whether the Egyptians built in brick at all, and he answers that temples, palaces and pyramids were ordinarily of stone but that brick is well attested for walls, fortresses and houses, especially in the Delta, that some pyramids were of brick, and that the making of bricks by foreign public slaves is represented on the monuments of the kings themselves. On the service in the field he cites the digging of canals and finds a trace elsewhere of labours connected with irrigation.
15:
Whether the midwives were Hebrew or Egyptian is the question of the passage, and three answers stand side by side. Gill sets out the case for Egyptians — an ancient historian says so, they were the women the king could likeliest prevail with, and their later answer about the Egyptian women reads that way — then decides against it, because the names are Hebrew, because the text calls them Hebrew midwives and not the midwives of Hebrew women, and because a nation would hardly employ foreign midwives. Ellicott says the Hebrew construction will bear either rendering and lays the arguments out without choosing: for Egyptians, that no king would expect Hebrew women to help exterminate their own race; against it, the Semitic form of both names and the likelihood that so numerous and peculiar a people had accoucheurs of their own. Wesley decides the other way, that they are called Hebrew midwives not because they were Hebrews but because the Hebrews commonly employed them, and that being Egyptians the king hoped to prevail with them. Clarke's argument assumes the opposite of Wesley's: they refused, he says, because being Hebrews they must have known the prohibition of bloodshed given long before the law. Clarke and Wesley agree only that the two named women were chiefs over others, Clarke citing an estimate of not fewer than five hundred midwives among the people.

The word rendered stools defeats them all in the same way. Clarke calls it difficult, occurring nowhere else but in one prophet where it is rendered the potter's wheels; since the root means a stone it has been taken for a trough in which the newborn was washed, but he reports a rabbinic derivation from the word for children, yielding when ye see that the birth is broken forth. Ellicott renders it literally as upon the two stones, rejects the suggestion that the modern Egyptian birth-chair is meant, since that seat is not made of two stones and there is no evidence of its ancient use, and calls very tempting an emendation reading the word as children — the solution Clarke had found in the rabbis, credited here to a modern. Wesley passes it off as seats used on the occasion.

On the refusal itself the accounts run from the general to the particular. Ellicott says only that the midwives, whether Hebrew or Egyptian, believed in a God who punishes wrongdoing; Keil notes that the God they feared is named as the personal and true one; Gill says they durst not take away human life against God's express law; Wesley that they dreaded his wrath more than Pharaoh's. Calvin goes further than any. Moses does not mean they were then first touched with the fear of God, but assigns it as the reason reverence outweighed the command; and they refused not merely because the crime was cruel but because religion flourished in their hearts, knowing the seed of Abraham was chosen and having seen it blessed, so that to extinguish the grace of God in it would be gross impiety — and he distinguishes this fear from the mere dread of punishment.

Two set the crime in a wider frame. Calvin ranks it against history and finds no parallel: children have been killed in the sack of a city, or by an uncle or guardian ambitious to reign, or to destroy the memory of a tyrant's house, but no such example of inhumanity has been seen since the world began. Henry asks why the grown men were not attacked instead, against whom some pretext might have been found, and answers that there is more cruelty in the corrupt heart than one would imagine, the enmity against the seed of the woman stripping men of humanity itself.
18:
Calvin allows the king no credit for the change of method: he was not reduced to a more moderate course by equity or mercy, but because he dared not openly expose the infants to slaughter lest the atrocity rouse the Israelites to vengeance — restrained, Calvin judges, by fear of rebellion rather than by shame.

The midwives' answer then divides the commentators as sharply as anything in the chapter. Clarke denies flatly that there was a lie in it. Women accustomed to hard labour, especially in the open air, have comparatively little pain in parturition, and the whole nation was then at mortar and brick; so with the strictest truth the midwives might say what they said. He has seen it himself, a labouring woman delivered between one afternoon in the field and the next morning's work. He answers the charge that the midwives told palpable lies and God commended them for it: there was neither lie direct nor prevarication: they stated a fact in the face of danger, and one the king had a thousand means of checking. Wesley sees no reason to doubt the truth of it either, and adds that the midwives, concluding the easy births to be the finger of God, were emboldened by them to disobey. Ellicott withholds the acquittal: this was probably true, but it was not the whole truth; having courage to disobey the king they had not the courage of their convictions, and took refuge in a half truth, pretending that what really occurred in some cases only was a general occurrence. Keil takes the reply as a deception that succeeded, childbirth being remarkably rapid among Arabian women. Gill reports both readings without settling between them — some think they told truth though not all the truth, others that they made a glorious confession of their faith, so Lightfoot, who takes the midwives to be Egyptians. Calvin alone convicts them: two vices are to be observed, since they neither confessed their piety with proper ingenuity and, what is worse, escaped by falsehood. He refuses the whole category of the serviceable lie, since whatever is opposed to the nature of God is sinful; both points must be admitted, that the two women lied and that in lying they sinned.

What then was rewarded? Keil quotes Augustine: not their falsehood but their kindness, and for the sake of what was good God forgave what was evil. Ellicott says the same — not because they equivocated and deceived the king, but because they feared God enough to disobey him and run the risk of a discovery that would have cost them their lives. Calvin turns it into doctrine: God in paternal indulgence values his children's works as if they were pure, though no action is so perfect as to be free from stain. Clarke, having no lie to explain away, says only that God was pleased with their frankness and blessed them for it.

The houses divide them again. Keil, Wesley and Ellicott read them as families given to the midwives, Keil setting to make a house in 2 Samuel 7:11 beside to build a house in the same chapter, Ellicott adding that there is no indication the houses were Hebrew ones. Calvin denies the clause is about the women at all: the pronoun is masculine, the idiom elsewhere always means a stable line or dignity, and it is unsuitable to the female sex that a woman be made head of a family — so God made houses for the Israelites, the plural marking the increase of separate families. Clarke gives the same pronoun argument, gives also the reply that the two forms are interchanged elsewhere, adds Shuckford's repunctuation making Pharaoh the builder who moved the Israelites out of tents so that no child could be concealed, and settles with Calvin on the people rather than the midwives.
22:
Gill takes the edict as the fallback after the midwives failed the king: a general order to all his people everywhere, and not, he insists, against every son born in the kingdom, which would have ruined it in time, but against those born to the Hebrews — the restriction supplied by the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan and by the Septuagint, which adds the words to the Hebrews. Ellicott knows the same addition and thinks it needless, since the context shows that only Hebrew children are meant.

Why the river? Clarke answers from Egyptian religion. The Nile being sacred, Pharaoh probably intended the young Hebrews as an offering to his god, with two objects in view — to secure a proper inundation and so the fertility of the country, and to stop the increase of the Israelites and in time procure their entire extermination. Ellicott reaches the same conjecture, but only after pressing two objections Clarke never raises. The Nile was viewed as a god, and to fill it with corpses might have been supposed a pollution; and Nile water was the only water drunk, so sanitary considerations might have been expected to prevent the edict. Perhaps then the children were offerings to the river, or to Savak the crocodile-headed god; and since the Nile swarmed with crocodiles throughout its course, the bodies were tolerably sure to be devoured before they became putrescent. He prefaces this with a catalogue meant to show the edict in no respect improbable: at Sparta the State decided which children should live, at Athens a law of Solon left it to the parent, at Rome infants were made away with unless the father interposed, the Syrians offered unwelcome children to Moloch and the Carthaginians to Melkarth, and Plato admits infanticide into his republic.

Clarke alone asks how long the order stood, judging that it was not made until after the birth of Aaron and was revoked soon after the birth of Moses; had it held in its rigour through the eighty-six years to the deliverance, the males could not have come to six hundred thousand effective men.

Calvin reads the escalation as judgment. Had the king not been transported with wrath and struck with blindness he would have seen that God's hand was against him; but the reprobate, once driven to madness, persevere obstinately, cruelty having tasted innocent blood growing thirstier for it. Finding his snares availed nothing, the tyrant flies to open violence, charging all the Egyptians with the work lest executioners be lacking. Calvin alone explains the daughters: spared so that, enslaved and allotted to Egyptians, they might produce slaves for their masters, while by them the races and names could not be preserved. He then turns the verse on his own century, where Antichrist leaves in peace those who deny Christ by treacherous silence, exercises no cruelty where he sees no manliness, and triumphs when a man who had some courage in professing his faith falls into cowardice.

Clarke closes by quoting at length Origen's second homily on the chapter, in which Pharaoh is the devil, the male children the rational faculties and the female the animal propensities, the two midwives the Old and New Testaments, and Pharaoh's daughter the Church gathered from the Gentiles, come to the water to be washed of the sins contracted in her father's house. Clarke denies the eminent man neither piety nor ingenuity, then rejects the method outright: if such exposition were allowed the trumpet could no longer give a certain sound, and every passage might be made to say something, anything, everything or nothing according to the fancy or caprice of the interpreter. He took his specimen from an ancient, he adds, to spare the moderns, from whose works he could produce many more absurd.
